title: Phrasal Verbs with Up: Ideas, Reactions and Difficulties
summary: Use up phrasal verbs to introduce topics, develop or invent ideas, express encouragement and saving, describe weather improvements and damage, and discuss relationships, repairs, tolerance, delays and confusion. Control separable objects and essential following prepositions.
learningObjectives: Distinguish bring up a topic, a topic coming up, come up with an idea and make up a false story.
Use cheer up, save up and clear up appropriately for feelings, money and weather.
Describe damage, separations, fastening, restoration and checking information with up phrasal verbs.
Express tolerance, delays and confusion accurately using put up with, hold up and mix up.

explanation.heading: Topics, suggestions and invented information
explanation.body: Bring up a topic means introduce it into a conversation; the topic can come up without a named person introducing it. Come up with a suggestion means think of and produce a new idea. Make up a story, excuse or claim means invent it, often when it is untrue. With separable verbs, say bring it up or make it up. With come up with, the idea follows with.
explanation.example: At the planning meeting, Sofia came up with a cheaper transport option.

explanation.heading: Changing feelings, saving money and improving weather
explanation.body: Cheer up means become happier; cheer somebody up means make them feel better. Save up for something means gradually put money aside to buy it; save up to do something gives the purpose as an action. Clear up describes clouds or rain disappearing and conditions becoming brighter. These meanings depend on the full expression and context.
explanation.example: After two grey days, the weather cleared up in time for our walk.

explanation.heading: Explosions, tearing and physical attacks
explanation.body: Blow up can mean explode, or cause something to explode. Tear something up means rip it into pieces; its past form is tore up. Beat somebody up refers to repeatedly attacking and injuring a person; it is a serious act of violence, not an ordinary argument. Keep the person or thing before up when the object is a pronoun.
explanation.example: The damaged container exploded, but nobody was nearby when it blew up.

explanation.heading: Separating, fastening and renovating
explanation.body: Break up or split up can describe a relationship ending. Do up clothes or shoelaces means fasten them; do up a kitchen or building means repair, improve or redecorate it, particularly in British English. The object changes the meaning of do up, so learn it as part of the expression.
explanation.example: The owners did up their small café before reopening in spring.

explanation.heading: Checking, tolerating, delaying and confusing
explanation.body: Look something up means search for information in a reference source. Put up with something means tolerate an unpleasant person or situation; with cannot be omitted. Hold somebody or something up means delay them. Mix somebody or something up means confuse their identity with another, and get mixed up can describe the resulting confusion. In separable expressions, pronouns appear between the verb and up.
explanation.example: A delivery problem held the installation team up for two hours.

comparisons.title: Mentioning a topic versus producing an idea

left.label: bring up a topic
left.example: Ada brought up travel costs in the discussion.

right.label: come up with an idea
right.example: Ada came up with a way to reduce travel costs.
right.note: Ada thought of a new suggestion.

left.label: come up with
left.example: The team came up with a useful proposal.
left.note: The team devised a suggestion they could pursue.

right.label: make up
right.example: The witness made up a story about the delay.
right.note: The witness invented an account that was not true.

comparisons.title: Different kinds of improvement with up

left.label: cheer up
left.example: The kind message cheered Leo up.

right.label: clear up
right.example: The thick clouds cleared up before sunset.

left.label: hold up
left.example: The road closure held the buses up.

right.label: put up with
right.example: Passengers put up with the crowded waiting area.

examples.sentence: The budget question came up after the main presentation.
examples.note: Came up means the topic arose in conversation.

examples.sentence: The journalist made up an excuse for missing the interview.
examples.note: Made up describes inventing an excuse.

examples.sentence: The class is saving up to visit a science museum.
examples.note: Save up to + infinitive gives the goal of putting money aside.

examples.sentence: A warm conversation cheered the anxious student up.
examples.note: Cheer somebody up means improve their mood; a noun object may precede the particle.

examples.sentence: Tara tore the out-of-date coupons up before recycling them.
examples.note: Tore up means ripped into pieces; a noun object can separate the verb and particle.

examples.sentence: After several years together, the couple decided to split up.
examples.note: Split up can describe the end of a romantic relationship.

examples.sentence: Please do your coat up before you step into the cold.
examples.note: Do up clothing means fasten it.

examples.sentence: I looked the unfamiliar expression up before answering.
examples.note: Look up means find information in a reference source.

examples.sentence: Two booking confirmations were mixed up at reception.
examples.note: Mixed up indicates that two things were confused.

commonMistakes.incorrect: They came up a better plan during lunch.
commonMistakes.correct: They came up with a better plan during lunch.
commonMistakes.why: Come up with an idea or plan requires with.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Please bring up it at the next meeting.
commonMistakes.correct: Please bring it up at the next meeting.
commonMistakes.why: The pronoun object appears between bring and up.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We cannot put up the loud music all night.
commonMistakes.correct: We cannot put up with the loud music all night.
commonMistakes.why: Put up with, meaning tolerate, must include with.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The assistant looked up it in the handbook.
commonMistakes.correct: The assistant looked it up in the handbook.
commonMistakes.why: Look up is separable; put the pronoun it between looked and up.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The unexpected traffic held up us for an hour.
commonMistakes.correct: The unexpected traffic held us up for an hour.
commonMistakes.why: With the meaning delay, the object pronoun must go before up.

studyTips: Make a four-way contrast: bring up a topic; a topic comes up; come up with an idea; make up a false story.
Learn phrases with their following words: save up for, come up with and put up with; avoid dropping required prepositions.
Practise object positions in pairs: bring up the issue / bring it up; look up the word / look it up.
Sort sample situations by function: feelings (cheer up), weather (clear up), delays (hold up) and confusion (mix up).

exercises.prompt: Nobody had a solution until Rosa ___ a practical suggestion.
exercises.feedback: Came up with means produced a new suggestion or idea.

exercises.prompt: The town centre was noisy during the repairs, and residents had to ___ the disruption.
exercises.feedback: Put up with means tolerate an unpleasant situation; with is required.

exercises.prompt: The documentary included an invented incident. The presenter had ___ the story.
exercises.feedback: Made up the story means invented something rather than reporting a true event.

exercises.prompt: During our discussion, the subject of parking charges ___ unexpectedly.
exercises.feedback: Came up means a subject arose in the conversation.

exercises.prompt: I cannot remember what this expression means, so I will ___ in an online dictionary. (look up; use the pronoun it)
exercises.feedback: A pronoun object is placed between look and up.

exercises.prompt: After hours of cloud and drizzle, the sky ___ before our picnic. (clear up; past simple)
exercises.feedback: Cleared up describes the weather becoming brighter.

exercises.prompt: Aisha wants a bicycle, so she is ___ for one. (save up; present continuous)
exercises.feedback: Saving up means gradually putting money aside towards a purchase.

exercises.prompt: A motorway accident ___ for nearly an hour yesterday. (hold up; past simple; include the pronoun us)
exercises.feedback: Held us up means delayed us. The object pronoun must appear between held and up.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Could you bring up it at tomorrow’s committee meeting?
acceptedAnswers: Could you bring it up at tomorrow’s committee meeting?
exercises.feedback: The pronoun it must come between bring and up.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We had to put up the construction noise for several weeks.
acceptedAnswers: We had to put up with the construction noise for several weeks.
exercises.feedback: Put up with means tolerate and includes the preposition with.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The weather cleared off by early afternoon, and the rain stopped.
acceptedAnswers: The weather cleared up by early afternoon, and the rain stopped.
exercises.feedback: The established phrasal verb for improving weather is clear up.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The receptionist mixed up them during registration.
acceptedAnswers: The receptionist mixed them up during registration.
exercises.feedback: Mix up is separable, so the pronoun them comes before up.

speakingExercises.prompt: At the meeting, Dana introduced the subject of the budget. Make one past-simple sentence beginning "Dana" and using brought up.
speakingExercises.feedback: Brought up means introduced a subject in discussion.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your team devised a solution yesterday. Make one past-simple sentence beginning "We" and using came up with.
acceptedAnswers: We came up with a solution.
speakingExercises.feedback: Came up with means developed a new idea or solution.

speakingExercises.prompt: A speaker invented a false story. Say one past-simple sentence beginning "He" and ending "it up". Use make.
speakingExercises.feedback: Made it up means fabricated the story.

speakingExercises.prompt: A song made Nora happier yesterday. Say one past-simple sentence beginning "The song" and using cheer + her + up.
speakingExercises.feedback: Cheered her up means improved Nora’s mood, with her before up.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your friend’s coat is open and it is cold. Tell them to fasten it in one imperative sentence using do up. Begin "Do".
speakingExercises.feedback: Do up your coat means fasten it.

speakingExercises.prompt: You see an unfamiliar abbreviation in a manual. Say one sentence beginning "I will" and using look it up.
speakingExercises.feedback: Look it up means search for the information in a reference source.

speakingExercises.prompt: Produce exactly two past-simple sentences using these facts. First: The traffic / hold us up. Second: The weather / clear up.
acceptedAnswers: The traffic held us up. The weather cleared up.
speakingExercises.feedback: Held us up indicates a delay; cleared up indicates improving weather.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the pronoun position and say the full sentence, changing nothing else: "I mixed up them at reception."
acceptedAnswers: I mixed them up at reception.
speakingExercises.feedback: The object pronoun comes between mixed and up.

listeningExercises.audioText: During the interview, Leena brought up the travel allowance, although nobody had mentioned it before.
listeningExercises.prompt: What did Leena do during the interview?
listeningExercises.feedback: Brought up means introduced the topic into conversation.

listeningExercises.audioText: Jamal saved up for several months and finally bought a second-hand camera.
listeningExercises.prompt: How did Jamal manage to buy the camera?
choices: He put money aside over time.
He received it as a prize.
He borrowed it from a friend.
listeningExercises.feedback: Saved up means gradually collected money towards a purchase.

listeningExercises.audioText: The engineer came up with a simpler method for organising the work.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word expression immediately after "engineer".
listeningExercises.feedback: Came up with describes producing an idea or method.

listeningExercises.audioText: The morning was dark and rainy, but by noon the sky had cleared up.
listeningExercises.feedback: Cleared up means the weather became brighter or less cloudy.

listeningExercises.audioText: Mina claimed that she had met the famous writer, but she made the entire story up.
choices: The speaker does not discuss its truth.
listeningExercises.feedback: Made the story up explicitly means the account was invented.

listeningExercises.audioText: We left home early, but roadworks held us up and we reached the station late.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why did the speakers arrive late?
listeningExercises.feedback: Held us up means delayed the travellers.

listeningExercises.audioText: The children tore up the old tickets before throwing them away.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word verb phrase immediately after "children".
listeningExercises.feedback: Tore up is the past of tear up, meaning rip into pieces.

listeningExercises.audioText: I cannot put up with the drilling noise from the building next door.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word expression immediately after "cannot".
listeningExercises.feedback: Put up with means tolerate an unpleasant situation.
